In complete AIS the external genitalia are completely female with a short/blind-ending vagina, gonads are mostly abdominal or inguinal, puberty brings feminization with sparse-to-absent secondary sexual hair, and post-pubertal gonadectomy is favoured. In partial AIS there is clitoromegaly, a narrow vagina and variable labial fusion, mostly inguinal gonads, breast development with slight virilization, and pre-pubertal gonadectomy is favoured. A blind-ending vagina with breast development but scanty pubic and axillary hair fits AIS rather than MRKH (which has normal pubic/axillary hair) or Turner syndrome.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q115, p.69

mcqs.question: 65 year old patient presented with moderate rectocele and urge incontinence. What is the initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Supervised pelvic floor exercise + bladder retraining

mcqs.explanation: Use bladder diaries in the initial assessment of women with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder. Encourage women to complete a minimum of 3 days of the diary covering variations in their usual activities, such as both working and leisure days.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q116, p.69,70

mcqs.question: Patient with a history of failed mid-urethral sling surgery for SUI. What is the best investigation?
mcqs.explanation: After failed continence surgery, urodynamic studies are recommended before considering further surgical treatment, to characterise the underlying bladder dysfunction (stress incontinence, detrusor overactivity or voiding difficulty).
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q117, p.70

mcqs.question: Pregnant patient presented with a painful swollen left leg. She was commenced on LMWH. How to evaluate her further?
mcqs.explanation: Compression duplex ultrasound of the symptomatic (left) leg is the initial investigation for suspected DVT in pregnancy. If the initial scan is negative but clinical suspicion of DVT remains, anticoagulation is continued and the scan is repeated.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q118, p.70

mcqs.question: Patient in labour with continuous fetal heart rate monitoring. At 4 cm dilatation, the CTG showed a baseline above 180 bpm. What is the best management?

options.label: E
options.text: evaluate the whole clinical picture and consider expediting birth

mcqs.correctAnswer: evaluate the whole clinical picture and consider expediting birth
mcqs.explanation: A fetal heart rate baseline above 180 bpm is an abnormal (pathological) feature. Management is not a single isolated action; the whole clinical picture should be evaluated. If the CTG trace is categorised as pathological: obtain an urgent review by an obstetrician and a senior midwife; exclude acute events (e.g. cord prolapse, suspected placental abruption or suspected uterine rupture) that need immediate intervention; perform a full risk assessment including a full set of maternal observations, taking into account the whole clinical picture, and document the findings; and consider possible underlying causes and undertake conservative measures. If the trace is still pathological after conservative measures: obtain a further urgent review, evaluate the whole clinical picture and consider expediting birth; if there are evolving intrapartum risk factors for fetal compromise, have a very low threshold for expediting birth.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q119, p.70

mcqs.question: Labouring woman was on continuous fetal monitoring with CTG. The trace showed variable deceleration with shouldering for 30 minutes at 7 cm dilatation. What is the next step?
mcqs.explanation: Regard the following as concerning characteristics of variable decelerations: lasting more than 60 seconds; reduced variability within the deceleration; failure or slow return to the baseline fetal heart rate; and loss of previously present shouldering. Variable decelerations WITH shouldering that persist for 30 minutes but have none of these concerning characteristics are not pathological, so the appropriate step is to continue the CTG.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q120, p.71

mcqs.question: Patient in labour with good descent and progression. CTG shows a baseline at 160, variability 2-4 for 45 minutes. What is the management?
mcqs.explanation: A baseline of 160 with reduced variability (2-4) for 45 minutes represents a suspicious CTG. If the CTG is suspicious and there are no other concerning risk factors: perform a full risk assessment (a full set of maternal observations and the whole clinical picture) and document; note that if accelerations are present fetal acidosis is unlikely; if the trace was previously normal, consider underlying reasons for the change; and undertake conservative measures. If suspicious with additional intrapartum risk factors (slow progress, sepsis or meconium): full risk assessment, conservative measures, obtain an urgent review by an obstetrician or senior midwife, and consider fetal scalp stimulation or expediting birth. With good descent and progression and no additional risk factors, conservative measures are appropriate.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q121, p.71,72

mcqs.question: A primigravida is in spontaneous preterm labour at 35 + 1 weeks of gestation. She has progressed satisfactorily and has been pushing for 15 minutes. Fifteen minutes prior to pushing, a suspicious CTG was noted. Baby passed meconium. You are not able to feel the fetal head abdominally and the vertex is at +1 station. Conservative measures failed to improve the fetal heart rate. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Expedite delivery by performing a caesarean section

mcqs.explanation: At preterm gestations, operators should be aware of a higher risk of subgaleal haemorrhage and scalp trauma with vacuum extraction compared with forceps. Vacuum birth should be avoided below 32 weeks of gestation and should be used with caution between 32+0 and 36+0 weeks. At 35+1 weeks with a suspicious CTG unresponsive to conservative measures, the head not palpable abdominally and the vertex at +1 station (mid-cavity), expediting delivery with mid-cavity forceps is most appropriate; ventouse is cautioned at this gestation because of the higher risk of scalp trauma and subgaleal haemorrhage.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q122, p.72,73

mcqs.question: Multiparous patient in labour with a diagnosed delay in delivery. Examination now shows vertex at +1 OA position.

options.label: B
options.text: Trial of instrumental delivery in theatre

mcqs.correctAnswer: Trial of instrumental delivery in theatre
mcqs.explanation: A vertex at +1 station is at the mid-cavity level. With delay in the second stage and the vertex at +1 in the OA position, a trial of instrumental (non-rotational) delivery should be conducted in theatre, where there is immediate recourse to caesarean section if the trial fails, rather than in the labour room, because mid-cavity deliveries carry a higher risk of failure.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q123, p.73

mcqs.question: Patient presented with ataxia, irregular menses and learning disability. Examination also showed cataract. What is the probable cause?
mcqs.explanation: This is classic galactosemia. Affected adolescents and adults often have focal neurologic findings such as tremor, ataxia and dysmetria (impaired ability to control actions). Together with cataracts, primary/premature ovarian insufficiency (irregular menses) and learning disability, the picture points to galactosemia rather than Turner syndrome.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q124, p.73

mcqs.question: Pregnant mother presented with absent fetal movements. Diagnosed with IUFD at 22 weeks. She chose conservative management and delivered at 24 weeks. How would you define this delivery?
mcqs.explanation: Stillbirth is defined by the gestation at birth, irrespective of when the death occurred. Deaths eligible for reporting to MBRRACE-UK: Late fetal losses - a baby born at 22 or 23 completed weeks' gestation showing no signs of life, irrespective of when death occurred. Stillbirths - a baby born from 24 completed weeks' gestation (or from 400 g where an accurate gestation is not available) showing no signs of life, irrespective of when death occurred. Neonatal deaths - the death of a live-born baby, born from 20 completed weeks' gestation, occurring before 28 completed days after birth. Here the intrauterine death occurred at 22 weeks but the baby was delivered at 24 weeks, so by gestation at birth it is classified as a stillbirth.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q125, p.73

mcqs.question: Patient on methadone collapsed with pinpoint pupils. What is the management?
mcqs.explanation: Give intravenous naloxone. The British National Formulary (BNF) recommends reversing acute opioid/opiate overdose in adults by intravenous injection of naloxone 400 micrograms to 2 mg; if there is no response, repeat at intervals of two to three minutes to a maximum of 10 mg. Doses used in acute overdose may not be appropriate for opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation in palliative care or chronic opioid use, where the recommended IV dose is 100 to 200 micrograms (1.5 to 3 micrograms/kg), with subsequent 100 microgram doses every two minutes if the response is inadequate. Careful monitoring of vital observations and maintenance of pain relief are still required.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q126, p.73,74,75

mcqs.question: Patient on 70 ml of methadone was observed to be lost from the ward and found unconscious near the toilet. Examination showed a weak and thready pulse. How to manage?
mcqs.explanation: This is opioid (methadone) overdose causing reduced consciousness and cardiovascular compromise (weak, thready pulse). The management is intravenous naloxone, an opioid antagonist; adrenaline is not the treatment for opioid overdose. Naloxone is given by the intravenous route (preferred) for its quicker onset of action and is titrated to response. Emergency treatment of opioid overdose: initial dose 400 micrograms IV; if no response after 1 minute give 800 micrograms; repeat 800 micrograms after a further minute if still no response; if still no response give 2 mg (up to 4 mg in a seriously poisoned patient), then review the diagnosis.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q127, p.75

mcqs.question: How will you monitor an early-onset FGR fetus growing at the 3rd centile with an absent umbilical artery Doppler?

options.label: D
options.text: Alternate days: umbilical artery doppler - DV and cCTG

mcqs.correctAnswer: Alternate days: umbilical artery doppler - DV and cCTG
mcqs.explanation: In early-onset FGR the intensity of surveillance is guided by the severity of the Doppler abnormality. Absent end-diastolic flow (EDF) in the umbilical artery is a pre-critical finding. Borderline (UA PI >95th centile, DV PIV raised >95th centile): repeat umbilical artery Doppler, DV Doppler and CTG every week. Pre-critical (absent EDF in the UA, absent DV a-wave): alternate daily umbilical artery Doppler and DV Doppler and CTG. Critical (reversed EDF, reversed DV a-wave): daily cCTG and/or DV Doppler. For an early FGR fetus at the 3rd centile with absent umbilical artery EDF (pre-critical), monitoring is on alternate days with umbilical artery Doppler, DV Doppler and cCTG. Timing of delivery in early FGR (gestational age up to 32 weeks): with AEDF or REDF in the UA, monitor every 2-3 days with cCTG and/or DV unless delivery is indicated; deliver if the DV a-wave is at or below baseline, or if short-term variation (STV) is below threshold (<2.6 ms at 26+0 to 28+6 weeks; <3.0 ms at 29+0 to 31+6 weeks).
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q128, p.75,76

mcqs.question: Early-onset FGR with reversed EDF. How will you monitor?

options.label: D
options.text: Alternate every 2-3 days: umbilical artery doppler

mcqs.explanation: Umbilical artery Doppler changes are defined as: PI above the 95th centile (borderline), absent end-diastolic flow (EDF) (pre-critical) and reversed EDF (critical). Ductus venosus Doppler changes are defined as: PIV raised above the 95th centile (borderline), absent 'a' wave to baseline (pre-critical) or reversed 'a' wave (critical). Depending on severity, repeat ultrasound (umbilical and ductus venosus Doppler) and CTG monitoring is normally undertaken every week where umbilical Doppler changes are borderline, alternating daily in early-onset FGR with pre-critical umbilical Doppler changes. Where the umbilical Doppler changes are critical (reversed EDF), daily cCTG and/or ductus venosus Doppler are indicated, as sudden deterioration of the fetal condition may occur.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q129, p.77

mcqs.question: Patient comes for booking. Her TPPA is positive, RPR negative, with a past history of syphilis. How will you manage this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat for syphilis since RPR is false negative

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure her as this is previously treated syphilis

options.label: C
options.text: Retest again since this is early syphilis

mcqs.correctAnswer: Reassure her as this is previously treated syphilis
mcqs.explanation: A positive TPPA (treponemal test) with a negative RPR (non-treponemal test) in a patient with a past history of syphilis indicates previously treated (or resolved) syphilis, so reassure. Treponemal tests (EIA, TP-PA/TPPA) detect syphilis-specific antibodies, are reported as reactive/non-reactive and remain positive over time in most cases (used for new diagnosis and screening). Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) detect antibodies released due to infection, are reported as a quantitative titre (higher titres indicate a stronger positive) and decline over time (faster with treatment), and are used to monitor treatment response and distinguish re-infection from resolved infection. On serology interpretation, a reactive treponemal test with a non-reactive RPR is consistent with previously treated syphilis (or early syphilis where RPR is not yet positive); with a documented history of treated syphilis, reassurance is appropriate.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q130, p.77

mcqs.question: How will you manage a case of early syphilis diagnosed at 33 weeks of pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.text: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mu im single dose

options.label: D
options.text: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mu im weekly for 2 doses

options.label: E
options.text: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mu im weekly for 3 doses

mcqs.correctAnswer: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mu im weekly for 2 doses
mcqs.explanation: Benzathine penicillin is the treatment for syphilis in pregnancy, with the regimen depending on trimester and stage. First/second trimester: early disease (primary/secondary or latent <2 years) is 2.4 MU IM as a single dose, and late disease (latent/unknown duration) is 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 weeks/doses. Third trimester: early disease is 2.4 MU IM weekly for 2 weeks/doses, and the weekly regimen is used for late disease at all stages of pregnancy. Early syphilis diagnosed at 33 weeks (third trimester) is therefore treated with benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 2 doses.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q131, p.78

mcqs.question: What is the diagnostic marker for myocardial infarction in pregnancy?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac-specific troponin I and troponin T are the biomarkers of choice for diagnosing myocardial infarction. Recommended sampling times vary by assay, so local guidelines should be checked; a negative troponin at presentation does not exclude cardiac damage as it can take up to 12 hours for the level to peak. Troponin is not raised above the upper limit of normal in healthy pregnant women and is not affected by anaesthesia, prolonged labour or caesarean section, and is therefore the investigation of choice. In contrast, myoglobin, creatinine kinase and CK-MB can be increased significantly in labour. Troponin can be mildly raised in pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension and pulmonary embolism in the absence of significant coronary disease, but in pre-eclampsia the troponin level is never above the standard threshold set for MI.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q132, p.78

mcqs.question: What is the diagnostic marker of choice in anaphylaxis?
mcqs.explanation: Mast cell tryptase levels are the diagnostic marker of choice in anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis suggested by sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms, life-threatening airway and/or breathing and/or circulation problems, and skin and/or mucosal changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema). Exposure to a known allergen supports the diagnosis, but many cases occur with no previous history. Mast cell tryptase can help confirm the diagnosis: as a minimum, one sample should be taken 1-2 hours after the start of symptoms; ideally three timed samples are taken - as soon as possible after resuscitation has started (without delaying resuscitation), 1-2 hours after symptom onset, and 24 hours later.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q133, p.79

mcqs.question: Antenatal woman with a BMI of 34, at 40 weeks of gestation, came for ANC with mild dyspnoea. Examination showed SFH 46 cm. USG showed high-normal liquor and EFW 3.6 kg. What to do?

options.label: D
options.text: wait for spontaneous onset of labour

options.label: G
options.text: measure oral glucose tolerance before deciding on the mode of delivery

mcqs.correctAnswer: measure oral glucose tolerance before deciding on the mode of delivery
mcqs.explanation: The large symphysis-fundal height (46 cm at 40 weeks), high-normal liquor and estimated fetal weight of 3.6 kg in a woman with a raised BMI raise suspicion of macrosomia/LGA and gestational diabetes, so an oral glucose tolerance test should be arranged before deciding on the mode of delivery. Polyhydramnios can be defined with gestational-age-specific thresholds, but generally a constant value of AFI >=25 cm or DVP >=8 cm is used across all gestational ages; by AFI it is classified as mild (25.0-29.9 cm), moderate (30-34.9 cm) or severe (>35 cm). Pathway for suspected LGA/macrosomia: SFH >90th centile leads to considering USS; if LGA/macrosomia is diagnosed, offer OGTT (refer to the diabetic team if positive), explain the limitations of USS in predicting LGA, discuss the potential risks of LGA for mother and baby, then discuss management options (expectant management, induction of labour, or caesarean section).
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q134, p.79,80

mcqs.question: A woman in her postpartum, who returned from a tropical country, brought in a baby with multiple skin pigments, microcephaly and hypoplasia of a limb. She had a fever with a vesicular rash in the earlier part of her pregnancy. What is the probable cause?
mcqs.explanation: Maternal varicella (chickenpox) or serological conversion in the first 28 weeks of pregnancy carries a small risk of fetal varicella syndrome (FVS), and the woman should be informed of the implications. FVS is characterised by one or more of: skin scarring in a dermatomal distribution; eye defects (microphthalmia, chorioretinitis or cataracts); hypoplasia of the limbs; and neurological abnormalities (microcephaly, cortical atrophy, mental retardation, or dysfunction of the bowel and bladder sphincters). FVS does not occur at the time of the initial fetal infection but results from a subsequent herpes zoster reactivation in utero, and occurs in only a minority of infected fetuses. A vesicular rash in early pregnancy with a baby showing skin scarring/pigmentation, microcephaly and limb hypoplasia is therefore due to varicella (chickenpox) rather than HSV, parvovirus, syphilis or CMV.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q135, p.80,81

mcqs.question: Postmenopausal woman came with a complaint of bleeding per vagina for two weeks. Hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy was done. Biopsy revealed hyperplasia without atypia in a polyp and the endometrium was normal (no hyperplasia). What is the management?

options.label: B
options.text: Follow up with endometrial sampling 3 months

options.label: C
options.text: Follow up with endometrial sampling 6 months

mcqs.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia confined to an endometrial polyp: complete removal of the uterine polyp(s) is recommended and an endometrial biopsy should be obtained to sample the background endometrium; subsequent management is according to the histological classification of the endometrial hyperplasia. Here the hyperplasia without atypia was confined to the polyp, which has been removed, and the background endometrium was normal (no hyperplasia), so no further treatment is required.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q136, p.81

mcqs.question: How will you follow up a complete molar pregnancy following evacuation? Her hCG has reverted to normal within 56 days.

options.label: A
options.text: Follow up 6 months from the day of evacuation

options.label: B
options.text: Follow up 6 months from the day of normal beta hCG

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge after two samples normal 4 weeks apart

mcqs.correctAnswer: Follow up 6 months from the day of evacuation
mcqs.explanation: For a complete molar pregnancy, if hCG has reverted to normal within 56 days of the pregnancy event, follow-up is for 6 months from the date of uterine evacuation. If hCG has not reverted to normal within 56 days of the pregnancy event, follow-up is for 6 months from normalisation of the hCG level. Follow-up for a partial molar pregnancy is concluded once hCG has returned to normal on two samples at least 4 weeks apart. As this complete mole normalised within 56 days, follow-up is 6 months from the day of evacuation.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q137, p.81

mcqs.question: Bicornuate uterus is associated with which of the following?
mcqs.explanation: Unification defects such as bicornuate, unicornuate and didelphic uteri do not appear to reduce fertility but are associated with increased risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes, depending on the type of defect. Women with bicornuate and unicornuate uteri have an increased risk of first-trimester miscarriage (OR 3.4 and OR 2.15), preterm birth (OR 2.55 and OR 3.47) and fetal malpresentation (OR 5.38 and OR 2.74); women with uterus didelphys have an increased risk of preterm labour (OR 3.58) and fetal malpresentation (OR 3.7). The strongest association for a bicornuate uterus is with fetal malpresentation (OR 5.38).
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q138, p.81,82

mcqs.question: Woman is counselled regarding endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the risk of progression to cancer?
mcqs.explanation: A 20-year follow-up study found that among women with hyperplasia without atypia (previously described as simple or complex hyperplasia), the cumulative long-term risk of progression to endometrial cancer is less than 5% over 20 years.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q139, p.82

mcqs.question: What is the risk of CTPA over V/Q scan?

options.label: B
options.text: Higher risk of maternal breast cancer

mcqs.correctAnswer: Higher risk of maternal breast cancer
mcqs.explanation: While CTPA is associated with a low radiation risk to the fetus, it delivers a relatively high radiation dose (up to 20 mGy) to the mother's breast tissue, which is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer; the dose estimate for CTPA is 20 to 100 times greater than for V/Q scanning. The dose depends on breast size, the technique used and the woman's age (the risk being greater in younger women). Breast doses from CTPA can be reduced by 20-40% using bismuth shields placed over the breasts. Lung perfusion (V/Q) scanning should be considered the investigation of first choice for young women, especially if there is a family history of breast cancer or a previous chest CT scan.
mcqs.references: MRCOG Recalls July 2024 (Paper 02), source Q140, p.82
